sentences: Beyond a great stone archway, a vast room opens up.
Under a lofty ceiling stands a wooden study, and a scholar in red sits inside it with a book open before him.
It feels as if we are peeking into a doll's house.
This is Saint Jerome in his Study, painted around 1475 by Antonello da Messina, an artist from Sicily.
It is oil on a limewood panel, only about 46 centimetres high and 36 centimetres wide.
The National Gallery in London has owned it since 1894.
Jerome was a scholar and monk who lived in the fourth century.
His translation of the Bible from Greek into Latin, known as the Vulgate, is still used by the Catholic Church today.
Here he works quietly at his desk, absorbed in his reading.
Look at the shelves around the desk.
Books, a ceramic vase and a jar stand there like tiny still lifes.
Rough or shiny, cold or warm, every surface seems close enough to touch.
This is the result of Antonello's skill with oil paint.
He learned this skill by studying the paintings of the Netherlands, where artists had mastered oil paint.
The picture was long thought to date from his stay in Venice, though some scholars now read it as painted in Messina in 1474.
Either way, his way of using oil had a huge influence on the painters of Venice.
That is why something curious happened.
In 1529 the Venetian connoisseur Marcantonio Michiel saw this painting in the house of the collector Antonio Pasqualino and wrote about it.
People were then unsure whether it was by Antonello or by the Netherlandish masters Jan van Eyck or Hans Memling.
It was firmly given to Antonello only in 1856.
Now look at the ledge at the bottom of the arch.
A partridge and a peacock stand there.
In Christian tradition the partridge is often read as a sign of truth, and the peacock as a sign of immortality.
Look into the shadowy hall on the right.
A lion is padding toward us.
According to legend, Jerome pulled a thorn from a lion's paw, and the grateful animal never left his side.
Somewhere in the room, a cat is curled up as well.
Do not miss the view outside.
Through the windows at the back, green fields, hills and a river unfold in miniature.
The light has been carefully arranged so that it gathers on the saint's chest and hands.
In time the painting left Venice for England, where it belonged to the Baring family of the Earls of Northbrook before it came to the National Gallery.
Step back and see the whole panel.
In this small picture, architecture and nature, learning and faith all fit together.
Today, think for a moment about where your own quiet study is, the place where a scholar in you can sit and read.
